Uniform title: Āścaryayogamālā Main title: Āścaryayogamālā with the commentary Laghuvṛtti Secondary title: Yogaratnamālā
Secondary Title: *Yogaratnāvalī* Author: Nāgārjuna Commentator: Guṇākara
Manuscript: NGMCP 1-33, reel number B-114/19

Description: *Āścaryayogamālā* (also known as *Yogaratnāvalī* or *Yogaratnamālā*, "The Rosary of Astonishing Yogas") by Nāgārjuna, accompanied by a brief commentary (*laghuvṛtti*) by Guṇākara, a Śvetāmbara Jaina scholar. This Nāgārjuna is renowned as the author (or namesake of various authors) of works on the six types of magical rites (*ṣaṭkarma*). A manuscript in the Asiatic Society in Bombay dates the composition of the work to 1240 CE. According to the text, it was written to serve the needs of people and to delight them. It treats standard subjects of magic, beginning with subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), followed by the immobilization of enemy armies (*stambhana*), the slaying of enemies (*śatrumāraṇa*), the attraction of women (*ākarṣaṇa*), and methods for attaining various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) through the preparation of medicinal elixirs (*rasāyana*), which the text describes in detail, as well as through mantras.
Notes: Revision 0: December 17, 2013.
Country of Publication: India.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Having reflected upon various jewels of yoga— each accompanied by visible proof— drawn from the ocean of the Guru’s intention,
they are brought here and revealed, made manifest, in this *Yogamālā*. Among them, first,
the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*) is described.

"Sitabhānuviṭapamūlam" means: *sita* (white) refers to that *bhānuviṭapin* (the sun-branching tree), which is the *arka* plant; its root is known as *mañjiṣṭhā*. Together with *bhavanacaṭaka* (house-sparrow), *gṛhacaṭaka* (domestic sparrow), and *śiraḥkuṣṭha*—these four medicinal substances being finely ground into powder and smeared with blood from one's own body-wounds, mixed with the blood of one's own limbs.
By placing prepared medicinal pills into food or drink, they bring even the three worlds under their control; how much more so a single man? || 1 ||
With the root of the white-flowered *vitapa*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, house-sparrow, and *kuṣṭha*—anointed with the blood from one's own body wounds—one brings the three worlds under one's control. ||1||
In this treatise, all the practiced yogas have been taught by the venerable master Nāgārjuna. Regarding "tāla":

on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one who possesses knowledge of realgar (*haritāla*) and mica (*śma*), having applied a mark (*tilaka*) together with *kuṣṭha* upon the mouth of a corpse, brings the three worlds under his control. (2)

The *tāla* [leaf] from a house of *piśācas*, obtained on a day sacred to the *bhūtas*, from the mouth of a *preta* and kept overnight, when employed by the Lord of Diseases, brings the three worlds under one's control. ||2||

1b) Regarding "the eyes of a dead man" and so forth: the eyes, tongue, forehead, heart, and nose of a dead man—these, when cooked in cemetery oil under a flower asterism, bring all queens under one's control. (3)
Oil prepared with the eyes, saliva, forehead, heart, and nose of a dead man brings all the wives of the lords of the earth under one's control when applied to the *karālaya* flower. (3)

Using human oil as the base, with a wick made from human fat and cloth, one should light a lamp at night on a human skull at the trunk of an *aśvattha* tree and collect the soot. By merely applying that [ointment],
one brings under control whomever one looks upon.
Thus ends the section on subjugation.
O best of pretas, the collyrium produced on the peak of Mount Mahendra from the lamp-light of the night—using human oil as the wick and the earth as the vessel—is the subduer of the world. || 4 ||
Thus ends the section on subjugation. Now, the procedure for causing enmity.

Now, regarding the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*): "O enemy of serpents" (*uragāri*). Having prepared incense from the head of a peacock and the head of a cock, one should offer it in the house or dwelling of a person; it destroys the affection of the beings residing there.
This excellent incense, produced from the heads of the enemy of serpents and the red-crested cock, reaches all dwellings within the three worlds.
It quickly destroys affection. ||5||

2a) Regarding the phrase "the woman who is both menstruating and unfortunate": for seven days starting from the day of her menstrual period, one should cast white mustard seeds into the womb of that unfortunate woman; subsequently, with those drawn-out [seeds] soaked in sour gruel (*śukta*), he who—
Whoever is touched by it becomes full of hatred. ||6||
[One should use] flowers that have remained for seven days in the flower-chamber of a woman who is menstruating and unfortunate.
Touched by white mustard seeds, who in the three worlds would not fall into enmity? ||6||

Regarding the phrase "fearing the two-legged and the two-humped": incense prepared from the wings of a crow and an owl by the most excellent practitioners destroys the affection of all things, both stationary and moving; how much more so a single house? ||7||
The incense produced from the resin of the *pīkadīva* tree, when employed, destroys the suffering of the circle of all moving and stationary beings, including those headed by kings. ||7||
"O armor of the lordly serpent! This incense, prepared from equal parts of the slough of a primary serpent and peacock feathers, causes even the three worlds to be driven into enmity. (8)
Thus ends the rite of inciting hatred.

This incense, born from the armor of the lord of serpents (Śeṣa) and joined with the wing-feathers of the enemy of serpents (Garuda), causes hatred among the three worlds as soon as it is employed. ||8||
Thus ends the rite of inciting hatred. Now follows the rite of eradication.

Now, the rite of expulsion (*uccāṭana*): "In the hole of a horse's hoof" means that having placed these two together— the head of a black snake and the tongue of a mad cock— into the opening of a donkey's hoof, and burying it at the door of whichever house, one causes that house to be expelled [from its inhabitants] within seven days.
Placed within the hole made by a horse's hoof, accompanied by the water from the tip of the tongue of an elephant's head,
and buried at the threshold of one's house, it causes an enemy to vanish within seven days.

Regarding the phrase "halinī-varāhavarcaḥ": having combined these four—lāṅgalī, boar dung, a corpse's hair, and camel bones—and burying them at the door of a house, that house is expelled [from its inhabitants] within seven days. ||10||
Halinī has the luster of a boar, long hair like a corpse, and the bones of the earth.
The best of yogis can clearly cause even the three worlds to vanish within seven days. ||10||

Regarding the phrase "the man with the staff and tax-collector": one should meditate on that man who is urged by the staff-bearer holding a club in his hand; being struck by him, [the practitioner] becomes one who moves swiftly in the form of barley, having emerged as a long-necked camel, and mounted upon that camel—thus visualizing such a person, even Bṛhaspati.
Within seven days, he causes [the enemy] to be eradicated; how much more so an ordinary man? ||11||

Having meditated for seven days upon even the preceptor of the gods as being mounted on the earth, having the form of barley, elongated, and impelled by men carrying staffs and taxes, one shall cause him to be driven from his place.

3a) "The bone of a dead man is a stake. The meaning is that if the bone of a man is driven into the threshold of a householder's door as a peg, his house becomes empty, like a cremation ground. ||12||
Thus ends the procedure for eradication. Now follows the visualization of one's own form in a mirror.
If the bones of a dead man are buried as a *śaṅku* at the door of one's house, that house will lose its prosperity and be destroyed by terrifying spirits and worldly calamities. (12)
Thus is the rite of eradication; now follows the visualization of one's form in a mirror.
"Regarding 'raktahayamāra': having cleansed and purified a mirror with red karavīra flowers, bhallātaka, and amlavetasa, one shall see the forms of a horse, a camel, and a cow. (13)
Having cleansed a mirror with red horse-radish, crimson flowers, bhallātaka, amlavetasa, and abhīru, one should look at it while assuming the form of a horse with a long neck and hooves. ||13||
The terms *hayagocarā* and *ahavānarā* are easy [to explain]. ||14||
[One should prepare a collyrium] from the bones of a horse, cow, boar, monkey, donkey, and camel, burnt in a crucible fire.
One should perceive their forms, as before, blended with the sound of frogs. ||14||

Regarding "with *añkola* oil and collyrium": having prepared a lamp with the oil from the seeds of the *añkola* tree and taken the soot (*kajjala*), one should mix it with cow’s ghee and anoint the eyes with that collyrium.
Puṣpanakṣatra, whose eyes were victorious, beheld in a mirror those various forms that he had assumed in other births. ||15||
Eye-salve made from flowers [treated] with milk fragrant with *aṅkola* oil [is beneficial].
One sees forms within a mirror as if they were in another existence. ||15||
"Anjitānayanā" (one with anointed eyes): having ground the fruit of *tagara* into a powder and mixed it with *aṅkola* oil, one should anoint the eyes with it.
She goes; the meaning is that she does not see a divine person. ||16||
Thus ends the observation of form in a mirror.
A person whose eyes are anointed with the paste of *tagara* fruit and *kola* sees a divine being; through the ointment of *tagara*, one attains the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Thus is the perception of form in a mirror.
Now he describes the concealment of a painting: "From the incense of a woman's placenta" (lalanājarāyudhūpāt).

By means of the incense from a woman’s womb-bed, a painting situated on a wall weeps visibly. Furthermore, by means of the incense of *guggulu*, the painting returns to its natural state; that is to say, it ceases from weeping. ||17||
Now he describes the disappearance of paintings:
"By means of the incense of *lalanā*, *jarā*, and *āyudha*, a painting on a wall comes to life visibly."
Furthermore, everything previously produced by incense quickly returns to its original nature. ||17||

Regarding the phrase "the female cat and the matron": by means of incense made from the womb-lining of a female cat (*mārjārī*) and the womb-lining of a preeminent woman (*pradhānastrī*), a painting situated on a wall is no longer visible. Likewise, by means of *suvarṇa*, *mahiṣākṣa*, and *guggulu* incense, even a painting that is not obscured—and which has returned to its natural state—is [rendered invisible].
It is seen. ||18||
The placenta of a female cat is not seen on a wall when treated with incense; however, O Kauśika, when fumigated with this specific incense, the painting returns once more to its original state. 18.

4a) Regarding "the camel-cheek powder": by applying a hand-salve made from yellow orpiment that has been repeatedly processed with the sweat, urine, and phlegm from a camel's cheek, various paintings on a wall do not fade; rather, they are drawn out by touch as soon as they are thrown [at the hand]. //19//
With *tāla* wood seasoned by the sweat from the temples of young elephants and by the urine of goats.
By means of that, one quickly draws forth various paintings from the application within the hollow of the hand. ||19||

He causes it to remember. Whatever—such as a tail or the like—is fumigated and enveloped with the incense of the *kukkurīgarbhaśayyā*, [the practitioner] shall take away or attract, by means of a needle (*kurcikā*) moved clockwise or counter-clockwise for a day, things of variegated colors and so forth; by moving it to the left, there is the release even of those that have been offered into the fire.
The meaning is "the process of returning to one's original nature. ||20||
Thus ends the *Citrāntarddhāna*.
A female dog with a tail wrapped around her body and emitting the smoke of incense removes delusion;
one should offer [oblations] with the left hand to Citravarṇa and others, for there is no liberation from the left side.
Thus ends the "Miraculous Vanishing."
Now follows the disappearance of humans.
Regarding "the stream, the moon, and so forth": *srotāñjana* (antimony from the river), *sevāla* (aquatic moss), *kaṇṭaka* (thorn-apple), *mākṣika* (beeswax), *madhuyaṣṭī* (licorice),

the blood of a maiden who has menstruated for the first time, fresh *lāṅgalī* (gloriosa superba), and *kesara* (saffron)— having made a pill with these medicinal substances, [placed] within gold, silver, or copper, there is the invisibility of a man.
He performs [it]. ||21||

A pill composed of *srotoñjana*, *śaśāṅkakantaka*, honey, and the first blossoms of *madhuka*, combined with fresh *halinī* filaments and placed within a core of the three metals (*triloha*), [achieves its purpose]. 21.

Regarding the phrase "nīlāṃśoka": having prepared a powder of blue *aṃśoka* sprouts infused seven times with the blood of a deer, one should wrap it in gold, silver, and copper and place it in the mouth; it effects the invisibility of the entire world, let alone that of a single person—this is the meaning. ||22||
Powdered sprouts of the *nīlāṃśuka* plant, processed seven times with the blood of a deer and encased within the three metals, when placed in the mouth, conceals the entire world. (22)

"North of the *tagara*": having become fire through the grasping of the moon, one should take the root that extends from the north of that *tagara*, wrap it in the three metals, and whichever man holds it in his mouth becomes invisible. ||23||

The root of *uśīra* from the *tagara* plant, extracted during a lunar eclipse while wearing garments of the cardinal directions, should be cast into the fire situated between the sun, the moon, and the fire, while it is visible. ||22||

Regarding "gorocanā": it refers to the flower of the *gauravṛkṣa* tree. When a woman has died by hanging, one should take the food and other remains from her mouth that were eaten by a bird called *akṣiro-māṇikākā*; having combined these medicinal substances with *gorocanā* and formed them into a pill, it should be placed in the mouth.
She makes a man invisible; she is known by the name Kalpalalanā. 24.

This pill, composed of yellow orpiment, the flowers of the *gudita* tree, the hair from the eyes of a dead woman, and the remnants of food eaten by a twice-born man, is the wish-fulfilling maiden of the senses. 24.

Regarding the phrase "in the cemetery" (*pitṛvana*): the meaning is that in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), a woman, having repeatedly rubbed realgar (*manaḥśilā*) upon her body at the time of her first menstruation, makes a mark (*tilaka*) with it; by means of this, a man becomes invisible. ||25||

Regarding the term "pārāvata": the *pārāvata* is a pigeon. Having placed black antimony (*kṛṣṇāñjana*) upon its thick neck and applied earth over it, it is roasted in the funeral fire (*citā-vaiśvānara*) until the earth becomes the color of fire. From the midst of that, one takes the roasted antimony and, with it—
One should apply collyrium to the eyes;
one becomes invisible. Furthermore, if one applies collyrium to the eyes with the blood of a black cat, liberation occurs.
The forehead-tilaka, ground repeatedly in a cemetery, combined with the semen of a young maiden and realgar, conceals even the three worlds when applied to the surface of the forehead. (25)
The *śrotacittikā* [mineral] from the belly of a pigeon is roasted in a sealed vessel (*puṭapāka*) with *nalada*.
He conceals the perfected ointment, and the black cats [conceal] liberation and nirvana. ||26||

Regarding the term *navaghana*: those which are both new (*nava*) and dense (*ghana*), namely young grass sprouts (*tṛṇāṅkura*), from which nectar has been extracted by blood—these are "new-dense-grass-sprout-extracted-nectars. It is said that the earth situated upon them is honey (*madhu*) and green orpiment (*haritāla*). By mixing these three with the lunar mansion of Puṣya and applying them as a tilaka on the forehead, one [attains success] even over the Siddhas.
He conceals it; how much more so from other men? ||27||

Thus ends the method of invisibility. Now, the wonders are described. Regarding the verse beginning with "bhramara": that peg produced from the root of a tree which is devoid of its core (sāra), being hollow within, when it is completely filled by living bees—that is, thoroughly filled by living bees—is [the means].

That which has a hollow interior within its womb is of such a nature that, when a stake is cast into space, it remains suspended in space; for how could there be a place for a world that is forgotten by all, unseen, and lifeless, within space? ||28||
Thus ends the method of making oneself invisible. Now, the magical performances (*kautuka*):
earth dug up from the roots of fresh clouds and lotus stalks, mixed with honey and *tāla* [palm resin], [is applied] to a flower.
He conceals them even from the Siddhas by applying a tilaka-mark upon the surface of his forehead. ||29||
Filled within its interior with bees, it remains placed in the circle of the sky;
though devoid of essence, this sprout born from the earth causes wonder in the world. (28)

5b) "A tree burnt by lightning" means: that stake which is a wooden peg burnt by lightning, smeared with moist, un-dried dog placenta together with the powder of black pepper, long pepper, and ginger.
The meaning is that when cast into such a space, it remains in that very space for a long time, measuring ten finger-breadths. ||29||

A lotus thrown into the sky remains suspended without support through the power of a ring on the finger of one whose hands and fingers are covered by a bed made from the placenta of a bitch, which was fashioned from the placenta of Saramā. This occurs simply by touching the finger upon which that ring is worn.
The meaning is that the lotus does not fall from the sky. ||30||
A wooden peg scorched by a crest of lightning,
when smeared with the moist placenta of a female dog mixed with the three pungents (trikaṭuka), remains suspended in the sky at a height of ten finger-breadths.
By the power of the seal, a lotus fashioned from the placenta of Saramā stands suspended in the sky upon the palm of the hand, independent of any support. (30)

Regarding the phrase "the seed-oblation of *staṃdrā*": *staṃdrā* is known as *āraṇikā* or *muṇḍī*. From the oblation of its seeds, in a fire that has been covered by a funeral pyre (*citā*), or in the sky from the rising of the sun, or even during the moonlight of the moon's radiance—the effect [of this practice] is such that they are seen. The Rudras, who bear tridents in their hands, appear in this manner.
In the Kṛta age, forms of Īśvara bearing tridents are seen. ||31||

"Kuru" means "perform. Take firewood consisting of soft wood, smear and rub it with sulfur and *kulutaila* oil, and then offer it into the fire with heated clarified butter (*ghṛta*). When that clarified butter (*ājya*) is offered, the blazing of Vaiśvānara occurs from the offering of those two [substances]. ||32||
6a) From the seed-oblation of the one called Staṃdra, [it occurs] in the excellent fire that has been piled up and covered.
In the moonlight, Rudras bearing tridents are seen clinging to it. ||31||
Place fuel made of *samidh* wood from the *kuru* tree upon a fire-pan smeared with fragrant oil;
then, by offering clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and molasses (*suta*), the blazing of the fire occurs. ||32||

"In such a vessel," as stated previously in the Āryā verse: when a vessel made of *asāra* wood, smeared with oil, is filled with wealth (*dhana*)—that is, mercury—in this manner, he asks what happens when sulphur powder is thrown into it.
He says: then, by the addition of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), it quickly ignites the fire. ||33||

"Kalmāṣikā" means crushed *vajra*. "Kalmāṣikā" refers to charcoal; with these, O King, fuel was prepared as before. Subsequently, as in the previous ritual application, when that fuel—consisting of firewood, heartwood, and fragrant wood—has been smeared with *sākula* oil, water is poured upon it for the oblation. Water.
From the oblation, the fire produced blazes intensely; indeed, the ignited fire burns completely. ||34||
In this manner, the mercury produced from sulphur-stone resides within the fuel.
Thinking, "The oblation must indeed be heated before the offering," he kindles the fire. ||33||
In the Kalmāṣikā forest, which was crushed and scorched by the fire of the thunderbolt.
The lightning fire, produced from the friction of water and wood, blazes intensely. ||34||

"Regarding 'ṛtumahyā' (the woman in her season): she is both in her menses and a young woman. That which has been perfumed—meaning it has been made to dwell or placed—for seven days in the flower-house, namely the womb, becomes perfected in due course. It is revealed as perfected through the lineage of the Gurus. He shows it in the midst of fire; when offered into the midst of embers, that heroic collyrium reveals a man."
In the midst of such a fire-pit filled with cow-dung ashes, by means of the oblation, the form of a person is seen.
Thus ends the chapter on curiosity. Now, the suppression of fire (*agni-stambha*). Regarding the verse beginning with "śaśī": *śaśija* is moss;

*jalaukā* and *dardura* are specific types of living beings (leeches and frogs). The roots of the *pāṭalā* tree, a specific type of tree—oil cooked with these medicinal herbs, when applied to the sole of the foot, [extinguishes fire] in the midst of a pit of glowing coals.

The meaning is that the practitioner wanders at will within the interior filled with glowing coals; he wanders through the house of flowers, which has been perfumed for seven days by the women who are like the spring season, and thus it becomes perfected in due order.
Through oblation into the midst of fire, one manifests the Sauvīraka person. ||35||
With these—hare's flesh, leeches, frogs, and oils—along with the roots of the *pāṭalā* plant.
From the application of the paste to the soles of his feet, the charcoal pit beneath him blazes. ||36||

He says: "Bheke ti. Having placed frog fat, mud, water-leeches, and moss into the middle of it, one anoints the feet and other limbs; thereafter, when walking over fire, there is no burning, cracking, or the like.
The meaning is that the fire becomes as cold as ice. ||37||

Regarding *dhava*: white frog-powder that has been repeatedly saturated with frog blood should be thrown into the fire; thus the fire is paralyzed and, even after hundreds of years, it does not perform the act of burning. ||38||
Frog-fat mixed with the juice of *śrāvaṇikā* and *ajaraloka*, combined with the essence of *caṃdrasaṃbhava*.
By applying an ointment to the soles of the feet, one makes even fire cold as ice. ||39||
One should dye with blood the dust arising from the limbs of a white horse.
Even by hundreds of years, the fire does not burn, for it has been paralyzed by him.

Regarding the word "turaga" (horse): even if fire is ignited by means of substances cast into the opening between the horse's hooves for a period of three months, it becomes incapable of burning even a single hair. ||39||
Thus ends the section on the immobilization of fire. Now, the immobilization of water.
Regarding the word "having thrown": the snake, having been rendered motionless by the *ḍiḍubha* mantra, is placed by those facing away from it into a piece of cloth smeared with its blood;
then, having been cast into the midst of water, it remains comfortably as if inside its own home. It is flooded by water, meaning that the immobilization of water (*jalastambhana*) occurs. ||40||

Even that food, though set ablaze by these—reed and cane roots, mice, barley, and frogs—placed within the holes of a horse’s hooves, does not burn me, for it has been rendered inert by the *stambhana* spell. (39)
Having cast Madana into the midst [of the fire] and entered the water along with Ḍiḍubhara, the wise one should remain within his own abode at will, as if inside his own home. 40.
"Śyona": he fills a pair of sandals with seeds of the *aralu* tree; having mounted them, he moves about as if on the ground, making his presence in the water clearly manifest. ||41||
Regarding "nine": butter, gold, and red ochre are well known; *durgandhā* is a specific medicinal herb;
and fish oil—by means of the powder of these, all the channels and apertures attached to the body are anointed, and consequently, one wanders upon the water like a fish. ||42||
Having made a powder of Śyonāka seeds, one should step upon a pair of sandals.
A man walks very clearly upon the surface of the water as if it were solid ground. ||41||
A man who has smeared his entire body with the oil and paste of fish, mixed with butter, gold, and red ochre,
wanders in the water like a crocodile.

Regarding "bhogeti": having ground *bilva* and *madanaphala* together with milk, one should form them into a pill (*guṭikā*), insert it into the hollow interior of a cow's horn, and keep it there for seven days.
Afterward, having extracted it from there, [one applies it] to the holes of drinking vessels or to the two holes of boats and the like.
Having cast the pill into a boat and so forth, one causes it to be immobilized. The immobilization of the boat and so forth becomes the immobilization of water.
Therefore, by this yoga, the water is immobilized; thus, because of the immobilization of the water, the immobilization of boats and the like is appropriate. ||43||
Thus ends the section on the immobilization of water.
Now, he describes the transformation into a *piśācī*: "With *jīva*... [and so forth]. It is the powder of *dhattūra* seeds;
the powder of the wood-worm (*ghuna*) found within dry wood; and the powder of *nīla*, *sthūlā*, *mācchikā*, and *kokilā*.

These herbs, when combined together and administered as a drink, turn one into a *piśāca*; that is to say, they make one appear as if possessed by a spirit. Likewise, this affliction is pacified by drinking molasses mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
From drinking these herbs, one becomes once again happy and restored to health. ||44||
A pill made from the pulp of bilva fruits ground with milk and inserted into the ear canals of an elephant causes its trunk to become paralyzed; this pill enters all the internal channels.
And they were filled with the pollen stirred up by the swaying of the trees, which are more golden than living beings, and with the songs of cuckoos.
The female ghosts (pretakī) lead a man away by means of a rope and a club. ||44||

Regarding the term "dvija": the hair of a Brahmin, a cat, a monkey, a Cāṇḍāla, an owl, and a mongoose—these, when ground together with cat excrement and administered in food or drink, produce madness.
[This is] the fourth group of four. ||45||

"Gome" means: having joined together the tail of a jackal and the two feathers from the right side of a crow, if these are placed upon someone's bed, that person is seized by a violent form of epilepsy (apasmāra). ||46||
The feathers and fur of a twice-born man, a cat, a monkey, a dog, a crow, a crane, and a mongoose.
Like flour ground by the incessant roar of the ocean, [it was the end] for all the worlds. ||45||
The *jāṅgula* medicine of a jackal, combined with the right wing-feather of a twice-born bird, when placed upon a bed, dispels the terrible epilepsy of an enemy. (46)

Regarding "ka-na": datura, yellow orpiment, citron, pigeon dung, peacock dung, and dog dung—these medicinal substances, having been ground together into a powder, when given to someone to eat or when the powder is sprinkled on their head, that person is seized by madness; the meaning is that they become insane.
Even an ordinary man becomes free from intoxication by the shaving of his head; for when the hairs situated on the head are shorn away, he then abides in the nature of pure being (sat). 47.
Thus ends the section on the transformation into a piśācī.

He speaks of the *romaśātana* (the removal of body hair): "Hālāhala," etc. The tail of a black cobra, having been soaked in *dhattūra* oil for seven days, causes the removal of body hair, head hair, and so forth. [The body] anointed with this oil...
The hair of the body and other such parts fall off of their own accord; for this very reason, this is the primary method for removing body hair. ||48||
Of the golden *ālābu* gourds, *mātuluṅga* citrons, *ijyāra*, *avataka*, peacocks, and cocks.
It makes one intoxicated even once; because it causes the hair to stand on end while free from intoxication, it is called *Keśī*. ||47||
A collyrium made from *hālāhala* [poison] and *lāṅśūla*, kept for seven days in gold-infused oil.
It removes hair and destroys affliction; this is the truth, the most excellent destroyer of hair. ||48||

Regarding the word "bahuśaḥ" (many times): having soaked sesame seeds with cow's milk many times, one should extract the oil from them; when the hair is anointed with that oil, the hair becomes white. However, the body must not be anointed with it; if the body were anointed with the oil, the body would become pale. He...
The meaning is that leprosy will manifest itself. ||49||
Regarding "eight": take one part of well-known lime (sudhā) and one part of yellow orpiment (haritāla); having mixed these together with water, they should be applied over a fire.
Afterwards, when it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, it is used to anoint the mass of hair;
then one no longer sees the mass of hair.
By this method, when applied with yellow orpiment (haritāla), the lime (sudhā) truly causes the mass of hair to fall out;
the meaning is that this is well-known in the world of both the moving and the non-moving. ||50||
By massaging the hair with sesame oil that has been infused many times with vajrī milk.
The hair on the body constantly becomes as white as the light of the afternoon sun. ||49||
Heated by fire with nectar-water mixed with one-eighth part.
Having recognized the web of hair, he moved through the world of the moving and the unmoving.
The passage beginning with "saindhava-haritāla" and so forth is easy to understand. ||51||
Thus ends the section on the removal of body hair. Now follows the immobilization of weapons (*śastrastambha*). "Having thrown," it is said.

8b) If the root of the *ahaṃsāsarapuṃkhā* plant, which grows in the northern direction, is placed in one's mouth, then for as long as that person does not speak even by remaining silent, no blow shall strike his body. (52)
Regarding the word "divase" (by day): on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight during a solar eclipse, or on a Sunday under the Puṣya asterism, one should cultivate the *pāṭalā* flower;

when held in the mouth, it paralyzes even one with a sword. The meaning is that blows from swords and the like do not reach the body. *Pāṭalā* refers to a specific species of tree belonging to the genus of the trumpet-flower (*jātī*). ||53||
A formulation consisting of rock salt, yellow orpiment, lime, and the juice of *yavanāla*—when applied even once—renders even the three worlds devoid of hair. 51.
Having cast [it] into the middle of the mouth, one should always [recite] the root-mantra followed by the Mahāhiṃsā-mantra during battle.
The weapon does not pierce his limb; it remains suspended in the air for as long as [he wills]. ||52||
On the day of the moon's eclipse or on a white lunar day (the 1st or 6th), having obtained the root of pāṭalā;
On Sunday, the day of Puṣya, one performs the Khaḍgavāra rite upon the face [of the deity]. ||53||

"By *parṇyā*" means that by this aforementioned method involving the seizing of the sun and so forth, the medicinal root of *śālīparṇī*, when placed in the mouth, wards off the terrible rain falling in the midst of battle;
that is to say, arrows do not pierce the body in the midst of battle. Not only that—
It has been obtained previously; it wards off the raining of *pāṭala* arrows. This applies as far as *parṇī*, *vīśāla-parṇī*, and so forth, which share the same meaning. ||54||

Regarding the *savitṛ-śastra-stambha*: having observed fasts for three days, when the sun sets on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha, the mantra—accompanied by *aśvagandhā* and yellow *siddhārthaka* (mustard seeds)—effects the immobilization of weapons against the Sun. ||55||
Thus ends the section on the paralysis of weapons.
Even leaves, when gathered according to this method and placed within the mouth, quickly ward off that falling rain of arrows from the battle. (54)
While the sun is setting, he offers oblations of fragrant substances.
Having stayed for three days, it is drunk according to the prescribed rite.
9a) On the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha. ||55||

Now, regarding travel to other directions: "With white *bhṛṅga*," etc. By binding these herbs—the root of white *bhṛṅgarāja*, white *kokilākṣa*, white *kākajaṅghā*, and white *śarapuṅkhā*, along with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and the seed-syllable of *bālaka*—around one's waist, one wanders upon the earth like the wind, just as the wind does.

"Going on the path": the meaning is that he too wanders about with medicinal herbs bound to his waist. Having applied the word "white," two feet should be smeared; then, free from death, he travels a hundred *yojanas* in a single day.
With white bees, with the cuckoo, with Kṣaṇajaṅghā, Puṃkhāśiphā, and the seeds of Hrī.
With these [clouds] bound to the slopes of his waist, he wanders over the earth like the wind. ||56||
Madanaphala, milk from a white-legged cow, and likewise milk from a single-colored Surabhi;
By applying the bark of the *bhūrja* tree to their feet, one shall travel a hundred [yojanas]. ||57||

Regarding "kaṅka" and so forth: *kaṅka* is well known as the chameleon (*kṛkalāsa*), *rakta-māla* is the owl (*ulūka*), their skeletons (*kaṅkāla*) are required; *aśvinī* is a specific type of insect called *surendragopaka*;

and *mayūra-rudhira* is peacock blood. Having prepared a pill with these medicinal substances and placed it inside gold, when it is cast into the mouth, one travels three hundred and fifty *yojanas* every day.
The practitioner proceeds, free from death. ||58||
Regarding "white": one whose eyes are white like a bamboo stalk; *āhaka* means a water-pot (*bhṛṅgāra*), and its roots are [the plant] *patera*.
These herbs, ground into powder and cooked with goat's butter under a lunar mansion associated with flowers (*puṣpanakṣatra*), are used as an ointment for the soles of the feet.
By this, the practitioner goes wherever he desires, day after day. This is the power of this ointment.
The meaning is that the practitioner attains the desired *yojanas*. ||59||
Thus ends the journey to a distant foreign land.
Now follows the observation of eclipses.

9b) Regarding "aṅkula": one should mix together aṅkula seed oil, peacock bile, and bhallātaka seeds; having blended these three, one should smear the surface of a mirror. Then, even at an improper time, a solar eclipse will be seen by people in the region of the sun.

When the surface of a mirror is smeared with the bile of a peacock, people standing even a *yojana* away perceive a solar eclipse; how much more so those who are nearby? By this, he demonstrates the power of yoga during the day. (60)

Regarding "muni-vṛkṣa": the *muni-vṛkṣa* is the tree of the sages, namely the *palāśa*; its flowers, their juice, and *śrotāñjana*—some say this refers to *rasāñjana*. Having reduced *śrotāñjana* to powder, one should apply it as collyrium to the eyes with the juice of *palāśa* flowers. By means of this, [one may see] a single star during the day.
He sees the collection. ||61||
Likewise, [one should take] the seed of *śikhi*, *vittāruṣkara*, and *aṅkola* oil.
By means of these, through the application of ointment, there would be the grasping and the seeing of the sun.
Ear-ointment made from the powder of the juices of flowers from the trees of the sages [is applied] to the blossoms.
He shows the multitude of stars to one traveling by day, like collyrium applied to the eyes.
Regarding "the lamp": first, one should prepare a root-wick that has been thoroughly saturated with lac juice;
having then saturated that wick again with silver-leaf oil, one should light a lamp with that wick, place it inside a vessel with a wide mouth, and position the vessel's lid over the lamp.
The monkey, having covered the principal vessel with a hide so that it was completely sealed, submerged it in water; the depth to which it sank became the measure for the lunar eclipse. ||62||
Thus ends the chapter on the eclipses of the sun and the moon.

Now, the procedure for possession (*āveśavidhāna*). Regarding the word "corpse" (*śava*): on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, guggulu resin is placed in the mouth of a dead body; drawing it back out again from within the mouth, it is ignited by the fire of a funeral pyre.
When the entire world is enveloped by that incense, it causes even the whole world to possess [the deity], let alone a single person—this is the meaning. (64)
10a) Having prepared a lamp with a wick made of lotus fibers, smeared with silver oil,
placed inside a large-mouthed vessel covered with a tiger skin; //62//

Just as that [reflection] occurs when it has entered the forest, and likewise when there is a particular lunar radiance; as long as they immerse themselves in the water, so long will there be the perception of the moon. ||63||
Kṛṣṇa, stationed within the cavity of the corpse’s mouth, illuminated the city with the fire of the funeral pyre.
On the actual day [of the ritual], it quickly causes the entire world to enter [the state of possession] through incense and other means. ||64||

Regarding "kanakāla": the seed of the *dhattūra* fruit, yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), *tribhuvanavijayā*, *citraka*, *ugragandhā*, *kukkuṭā*, and pieces of sugar—by means of the incense made from these medicinal substances combined together, one causes the world of the moving and the unmoving to enter [into a state of possession]. By this incense, [one effects the entry] of the world of the moving and the unmoving.
Possession occurs. ||65||

Regarding "mahiṣā" (buffalo): O child, having repeatedly saturated the powder of five-limbed dhattūra with buffalo blood, one should dry it and then use sixteen equal parts of it mixed with the poison of a snake; by burning this as incense at night, the activities of men are seized. ||66||
Thus ends the chapter on possession (āveśa).
Pieces of the eggs of the Citravaca and Kukkuṭa birds, together with gold and *alamātula* seeds, when fumigated, cause possession in the world of all things, both moving and stationary. (65)
Smeared with buffalo blood, consisting of five ingredients and mixed with a sixteenth part of poison,
along with a golden twig and incense, this rite performed at night brings about the destruction of men's desires.

Now follows the procedure for the application of poison. Regarding the term "white" (*sita*): the root of the white oleander (*śvetakaravīra*), the insect from the *arka* tree, the sting of a scorpion, and the venom of the *vatsanāga* snake—having ground these herbs with water and smeared them upon a hand-pipe, whoever is touched by it becomes as if bitten by a snake; he appears just like one bitten by a serpent.
The meaning is that it destroys its limb in an instant; by the trunk, [it destroys] the nose itself. ||67||

Regarding "kanaka": having ground these two—kapirakta-roma (red monkey-hair) and citrakūṭa-khaḍikā (tiger-iron)—and having infused them with the milk of the arka plant for seven days, one again forms a pill in the shape of a complete cloth-strip; by means of that [the following is achieved].
The meaning is that by means of those two chalk-monkeys, having drawn the form of a snake on the surface of the earth with a pill, whoever touches it appears as if bitten by a snake.
Thus ends the section on the administration of poisons.
The square root of the product of the [number of] horses (7), the beginning of the [number of] elephants (8), and the [number of] śarabhas (10) is the ārala of the scorpion;
when increased by its own square root, it becomes the karoga-nasa. 67.
An ointment made from *vānarī* and *ṣaṣṭikā* smeared with molten gold for seven days [is effective].
Touched by those two as they were written, the serpent on the ground became poisonous. ||68||
Now, regarding the administration of the anti-venom: *Malaya* refers to sandalwood and *nāgakeśara*, which are well-known.

Having combined these herbs—*madanaphala*, *kuṣṭha*, and *tagara*—into one, one should grind them with rice-water, drink the mixture internally, and apply it as an ointment externally on the site of the bite; it is effective against various kinds [of poison].
It destroys all poison—whether stationary, mobile, or artificial; the meaning is that it does not merely destroy artificial poisons produced by the previously mentioned methods. ||69||

"Like that": on that very same day, one should take the dung of a calf that has been born, along with *tagara* and *nāgakaṇṭaka*; having made a pill from these, one may thereafter consume poison as desired.
The defect of the poison will have no power over him, just as when Śūlapāṇi [Śiva] formerly began the churning of the ocean.
Just as the Lord consumed the Kālakūṭa poison according to his will, so too, no one would find fault with him for consuming it. ||70||
Combined with *malayabhavana*, *agakesara*, *madanaphala*, *vyadhi*, and *tagara*.
Indeed, this medicine, when combined with rice-water, destroys various kinds of poison. ||69||
On that day, having thoroughly consumed the excrement of a newborn calf along with pills of tagara, one may drink poison at will,
as if it were the [poison] of Śūlapāṇi.

Bheketi. Having ground together frog fat, the fat of a snake whose mouth has been turned away, *kaṭuka* and other substances, and tree fruits, one should smear the palm of the hand with it; by the touch of that palm, all poisons depart even from the site of the bite.

11a) Regarding "cow's ghee" and so forth: having ground together cow's ghee, the milk of a *surabhi* cow, peacock blood, pieces of flesh from a two-headed snake, and pieces of bone from a two-headed snake; |||
Whatever drum, kettle-drum, hand-drum, or similar instrument is smeared with this [substance], by its sound even the three worlds become free from poison. When a snake strikes,
one should then smear the faces of the hand-drums with these medicinal herbs and subsequently play the tip of the hand-drum.
The meaning is that there is the subduing of poison. ||72||
Thus ends the removal of poison.
Indeed, the frog, the two-faced one, the fat-bitter plant, and the fruits of the śleṣmānta tree [are used].
Having smeared one's hands with these, one removes poison through touch or from a bite. ||71||
Smeared with cow’s ghee, excellent peacock flesh, blood, the meat of two-headed snakes, and skeletons, and resounding with the cries of gods, it renders even the three worlds free from poison. //72//
Now follows the removal of irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).

Regarding the phrase "naked and so forth": on the fourteenth day, at the time of two *praharas*, having loosened one's hair and become naked, having tied a protective knot (*rakṣāgranthi*) upon the topknot and performed protection of the limbs, one should invoke and worship the eight guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*), consecrate the medicinal herb (*auṣadhī*), and [offer] incense, flowers, sandalwood, and so forth.
According to the prescribed rite, on a dark lunar day, one should take the root of that plant and divide it into seven pieces or seven segments;

having tied them with a thread dyed with turmeric and other colors, and subsequently binding them on the hands of those suffering from fever, they destroy—that is, remove—the quartan fever. Alternatively, the root of *jigina* [is used] as before.
Taken with buttermilk and drunk, it destroys even a most violent quartan fever. ||73||
Thus ends the offering for irregular fevers. Now, he describes the subduing of spirits, planetary influences, and the like.
The seven pieces of wood collected according to the rules for one who is naked and so forth.
On the day of Bhūta, they destroy quartan fevers by binding their hands [in the prescribed manner]. ||73||

11b) "Oṃ. When one seized by a planetary spirit (graha) sees this mantra— *oṃkāracakra hūṃ phaṭ*— written on the right hand of the practitioner with fragrant substances such as saffron (*kuṅkuma*), then the spirit [is subdued].

It perishes. This mantra is renowned as being called *ḍāmara*. It is truly the *ḍamara*—the end-maker—of spirits (*bhūta*s), such as *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *śākinīs*, and so forth. Indeed, there are many other mantras on earth [that require] great hardship through vows, fasts, mantra-recitation, worship, meditation, and the like.

All [these effects] are accomplished through successive traditions. This [charm], merely upon being seen, performs tasks such as planetary liberation (*grahamokṣa*). By way of context, one should wrap the right foot and wing of a moving owl with a white thread, as described previously for the right side. ||74||
With the placement of the syllables *oṃ*, *kāra*, *cakra*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ* upon the hands, this well-known mantra, Bhūtaḍāmara, effects liberation from the seizing spirits (*graha*). ||74||

Take *gogeti*, cow-horn, cat-dung, elephant-claw, *sarvakañcuka*, peacock feathers, *śatapuṣpā*, garlic, and asafoetida; having mixed these together, when administered to one seized by a spirit (*graha*), the spirit that has possessed them is released and perishes. According to others, it is called *bhujagavallī*; in their view, it is thrown into the midst of a snake-venom preparation.
The planets cry out; he cuts [them]. Thus, the planet-banner (grahaketu) destroys the faction of the planets; the meaning is that it destroys the ḍākinīs and so forth. *Durgandhā* is *śatapuṣpā*.
Thus ends the chapter on the liberation from planets seized by the Viṣama-hṛta.
By means of the yogava, the cat’s dung, the elephant’s tusk, the snake’s skin, the peacock’s crest, and the moon.
This incense, the banner of the planets, is combined with foul-smelling garlic and asafoetida. ||74||
Now follows the observation of the luminaries.
Regarding "Dharaṇī": having ground these three— earth, the body of a *bhūnāga*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and yellow orpiment (*haritāla*)—
the practitioner should perform an anointing of the body with mustard oil at night while [the lamp] is burning.
The body of the practitioner is seen by other people as if it were blazing. ||76||

Regarding the term *khadyota*: a firefly (*khadyota*) is a specific type of insect known as an *indragopa* (coccinella beetle). There is also oil from the seeds of the *āmalakī* fruit and oil from autumn seeds (*śarannabīja*). Within these two oils, one places the firefly and the *indragopa* insect. Having dried them and ground them into a fine powder, one should smear it; whatever body or form is thus smeared [becomes luminous].
There, at first, it is seen as if blazing and flaming. ||77||
Thus ends the chapter on the observation of luminaries.
A paste ground with earth, creepers, stone-juice, and mustard oil.
In the darkness that carries the luster of silver, he kindles this body.
If one is smeared even slightly at night with a paste made from the oil of glowworms, cochineal insects, cow-dung, hemp seeds, and sesame,
the body's impurities burn away.
Now follows the procedure for the application of collyrium.

Regarding the word "mṛga" (deer): having ground the eyes of a jackal with water and rubbed them together, one should gradually form two pills. Then, by means of these two—using the right eye of a jackal for the practitioner’s own right eye and the left for the left—the practitioner, with eyes thus anointed, will [overcome] many bhūtas at night.

He sees yakṣas, rākṣasas, and so forth; for that practitioner, the yakṣas and others appear and bestow the substances of accomplishment (*siddhadravya*), such as eye-salve (*añjana*), magical sandals (*paṭuka*), invisibility (*antarddhāna*), and the power of traveling through the sky (*ākāśagāmin*). ||78||
His pair of eyes was gradually anointed with the powder from the eyes of a rogue deer.
He sees many [beings] at night, and they bestow perfected substances. ||78||
"Paṭaha" refers to a specific type of drum (*vādyaviśeṣa*). "Having a lamp within itself" means that it has a lamp in its interior; [it is struck] with a very fine surface (*talena*).
A drum covered with a monkey skin—such as this, when placed in the middle of a house at night, surpasses the light of the moon; that is to say, it makes it appear inferior. ||79||

Regarding "cow's milk" and so forth: cow’s milk, *atibalā*, *kākahī* (well-known), *madhuyaṣṭī*, cow’s ghee, *balā*, *abalā*, sugar, and *matsyaṇḍī*—having ground these medicinal substances into a powder.
A drum, its interior filled with lamps and covered with a very thin green hide, standing in the middle of a house at night, surpasses the moonlight. ||79||
Cow’s milk, atibalā, and yaṣṭimadhu [are used for] ghee; balā and sugar [are used for] pills during the autumn season.
One should prepare an electuary (*avaleha*). Even a barren woman obtains a son who is a lord of the world at the time of the sacrificial rite (*kratu*).
"Lord of the world" (*lokeśvara*) means a great king who rules over the worlds. By performing this, even a barren woman conceives; how much more so, then, other women? ||80||

Regarding "Aśvattha": Under the Revatī asterism, one should take a branch of the Pippala tree (the holy fig tree) from a grove. Under the Revatī asterism, a barren woman should tie a thread upon her hand; thus the barren woman conceives a child. That tree which grows upon another tree is called *vaṃdāka*. ||81||
Having licked [the sacrificial oblation], she gave birth to a son who was a lord of the world of women. ||80||
Having taken the bark-extract produced from the Aśvattha tree under the asterism Revatī, [one should apply it].
A barren woman does not grasp a fetus with her hand, for she is incapable of bearing one. ||81||

Regarding "vyāghra" (tiger): tiger-blood, pieces of tiger-flesh, *bhramara* (a product of curd and milk), and *utpala* (a specific flower)— having ground these together and stirred them with water, if they are kept in the middle of a pit for a constant period of days,
on the seventh day, a pair of tigers with a lifespan of six months [will appear].
It arises. ||82||
13a) "Human" refers to the pair of human male and female; their impurity is that which has arisen from the body and so forth, as well as their blood, their semen, and likewise their earwax.

Having ground these medicinal herbs with the milk of a woman—the impurity of their eyes—and having wrapped them in a wolf-skin for twenty-one days, one releases them; after twenty-one days, a pair of man and woman emerges from among them. ||83||

In a vat filled with curd and honey, where bees were attracted by the flesh of tigers killed by other tigers, a pair of tigers sustained their lives for six months using seven *āḍhakas* [of that mixture]. (82)
Having violently crushed the human excrement, blood, sense organs, ears, and eyes, [one should prepare] with that liquid.
With these [substances] prepared with *sāhuḍa* and *kṛttikā*, a human couple shall [be produced] within twenty-one days. (83)

Regarding the term *lalanā*: if the root of the *dhattūraka* plant is bound to the waist of women even at the very beginning—that is, prior to sexual intercourse—it prevents conception (*garbha*). Likewise, if that same root is bound at the time of sexual union, it prevents conception; and if it is bound to the waist even during the period of menstruation (*ṛtukāla*), it likewise prevents conception.
The meaning is that it prevents pregnancy in women. ||84||

"Having consumed" (saṃbhajya): by consuming only aged clarified butter (*purāṇaghṛta*) during her menses at the proper time, and by constantly consuming aged, matured cow's ghee, even a woman who has engaged excessively in sexual intercourse will conceive a child. This applies even to a woman intent on frequenting the company of men at night.
The meaning is that by drinking aged cow's ghee at the [proper] time, one does not conceive a fetus. ||85||
The *mātuluṅga* root, tied to the hips of the *lalanā*, prevents [the flow] at the tip;
it is seen that this *puṣpaka* constantly protects the embryo during the time of sexual union. (84)
Having consumed only aged ghee at the proper time during their menses, women who are constantly devoted to sexual pleasure can arrest conception.

13b) It produces a nursemaid. When the powder of *puṣpanakṣatra*, the powder of *amalaphala*, and the powder of *sauvīrāñjana* are combined together and drunk mixed with cold water, then there is no fear for the fetus and no fear for the menstrual period (*ṛtu*).

A woman who is deprived of her husband and, during her fertile period (*ṛtusamaya*), desires pregnancy— precisely because of that dual state of being— wanders the earth like a fearless *araṇḍā* bird, engaging in sexual union as she pleases. (86)
Having drunk a powder of *dhātrī* and collyrium with cold water during her menses, let the woman afflicted by passion roam about, free from fear of pregnancy or her husband. 86.

Regarding the term *surapati*: a woman who, during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), drinks or licks the powder of the *indragopaka* insect mixed with water, [ensures that] her pregnancy and her fertile period remain far away; that is to say, they do not occur. The word "hi" has the sense of "because. ||87||

It causes [the penis] to swell. In whichever house these three—alaktaka (lac), indragopaka (coccinella beetle), and the fat of a tawny cow—are prepared and applied, there the genitals of the desirous men and women do not wither; that is to say, the penis, the vagina, and so forth do not perish. ||88||
If a woman drinks the powder of *surapatigopaka* with the juice of *ṛtumalla*, her pregnancy and hemorrhoids will indeed be driven far away. (87)
In that house where a lamp—prepared with pure ghee, fragrant resin, and reddened by fresh lac—is burning, there never occurs the breaking of a limb of a superior being. (88)

14a) Regarding "white arka": in whatever place a lamp is lit with a wick made from the cotton-fiber of the white *arka* plant, soaked and thoroughly saturated with the fat of a pig, there, for as long as the entire night lasts, [the woman] does not [satisfy] the man who desires her.
It falls and remains indeed motionless; this is the meaning. ||82||

Regarding the term *bṛhatī*: the powder of *kaṅkaṭārikā*, white mustard, *kuṣṭha*, *ugragandhā*, and *aśvagandhā*, when mixed with water and applied repeatedly as a paste to the penis after it has been reduced to the size of a seed (*akṣa*), and having been massaged, it becomes like that of a horse—that is, like that of a stallion. ||90||
A lamp made from a wick of white Arka-cotton soaked in boar fat holds fast the male organ throughout the night, even for a fragment. (89)
When smeared with these—bṛhatī, white mustard, vacā, and the fragrance of the four-legged [animal]—the excellent organ of that man becomes like that of a horse. (90)

Regarding the word "ghṛta": ghee, honey, sesame oil, the fruit of *kaṇṭakārikā*, moss, and *svayaṃguptā* should be placed in a copper vessel and kept therein for seven days; thereafter, by applying and massaging this onto the penis, its enlargement occurs. ||91||

Regarding the term "heard": having pierced a *karañja* fruit and inserted mercury into its center, one should then place the mercury situated within the *karañja* fruit and the root of white *sārapuṅkhā* into the mouth.
When sexual intercourse is performed, then, by the will of the man, his semen remains arrested for as long as desired.
When liberation is desired, then both of these, having been chewed and swallowed, result in the liberation of the seed.
Just as when cow dung that has been consumed and digested is later expelled along with undigested food,
like the stone from a jujube fruit, it emerges through a perforation.

Having joined the *dhārakīṭa* with the heart [mantra] and having joined the *rāsapucchaka* with *savaraka*, one binds these two together; when bound to the waist of a man, that man becomes paralyzed. ||92||
Ghee, honey, oil, the fruit of bṛhatī, śūkara, and mātmaguptā.
By these [substances], when kept for seven days in a copper vessel, there is an increase in the growth of the limbs. 91.
The seed of the white-banded snake (*sitavāṇapuṃkhitā*), joined with the fruit of the *karañja* tree and its root, when placed within the cavity of the mouth, causes paralysis at will. (92)

Regarding "ṣaḍviṃdhi": *ṣaḍbindu* is a specific type of insect; its body-born powder, the root-fiber (*śiphā*) of the long-branch *kharamañjarī*, and its powder—having combined these two aforementioned powders with *arka* cotton to form a wick, if that lamp is lit in the middle of a house...
In the midst of that house, the seed of men who lust after her becomes paralyzed. ||93||

Regarding "ājyam": goat's milk, cow's milk, and cow's ghee—having combined these three in one place and applying them as an ointment to the soles of the feet, the semen of men who desire [women] remains arrested for the entire night.
Thus ends the method for the immobilization of semen.
With the powders of the six bindus of the body and the roots of the rhizomes of *kharamañjarī*.
It obstructs the semen of men, like a lamp using the cotton wick of the sun. ||93||
By applying goat's milk, * * ?, and ghee to the pair of feet, this yoga arrests the seed of man for the entire night. (94)
15a) "Moist" means: when the moist, undried feces of a woman have been pierced with a scorpion sting and placed in the ground, and it is covered over with a layer of dust until—
During that time, the noble lady experiences a piercing pain in her womb; once it has been extracted, there is liberation. ||95||

Regarding *kuṣṭha*: for seven days, a *guñjā* seed dwells in the mouth of a black cobra; alternatively, for seven days, a *gīlikā* dwells in the mouth of a black cobra. Afterwards, having extracted it from there and administered it in the food or drink of an enemy, it causes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) when [taken] with a decoction of the five parts of the *piyāla* tree.
When eight parts remain, it should be drunk; thus leprosy (kuṣṭha) is cured. The decoction should be drunk for three days. //96//
Moist earth, a hole in the ground, a woman, excrement, a scorpion, and a lizard—[these are inauspicious].
It casts off terrible and intense suffering until that Lord is uplifted. ||95||
In seven days, it releases leprosy and consumption, having remained for a night in the mouth of a serpent.
Then one should drink a decoction of *guñjā*, *bhavana*, and *gojā* until it is digested. ||96||

Regarding "sakṛdantā": having written the name of someone with crow's blood using a stylus made from a crow's wing-feather on a crow's wing-tuft (*kākapiccha*), if it is thrown into the midst of that person's excrement, he will be swiftly destroyed by that very excrement and eaten incessantly by swarms of crows; there is liberation only when [the object] is extracted. 97.

Regarding this very point, he states a second application: "With the heart of a *droṇaka*," and so forth. Having written the name of one who is a *droṇaka*—a black crow—upon a leaf of a mango tree with its blood, and covering it repeatedly with its excrement, that person is constantly devoured by crows; there is liberation when [the leaf] is removed. 98.
O twice-born one, that name which is inscribed upon the leaf of the blood from the heart of the one who has cast off his body once and for all—
that very name the hosts of twice-born ones here devour incessantly. (97)
And on a mango leaf, upon which his name was inscribed with blood drawn from Dronaka’s heart.
That [food] hidden within its excrement is consumed by crows; she too [is consumed]. ||98||

Now, the method for killing cattle: "At the gate of the cow-pen. Having thrown a *kṛkalā*—a specific living creature—into a jar at the entrance of the cow-pen, it is buried in the ground and covered with dust on top.
By means of that, as the cattle enter and exit the pen, they step over the jar as it remains there. At that time, in the cow-pen...

The cows appear as if asleep or in a swoon; even when struck, they do not rise from their state, remaining as if sleeping as long as that pitcher is not drawn out from there. But once it is drawn out, the cows are free from sleep and move about as they please—this is the meaning. ||99||
The lizard’s escape resulted from leaping over the jar buried at the gate of the cow-pen.
Even when struck seven times, they do not rise as long as that [impurity] has not been extracted. ||99||
Now begins the section on the cessation and release of the fetus.

Regarding *mallaka*: for whichever woman is giving birth, if one prepares a vessel (*sarāva*) to cause the arrest of her labor, one writes the syllables of the *huḍu* mantra upon it and interweaves (*vidarbhitāni*) her name [with them]. Then, at that very moment, the woman’s labor is arrested. This is the meaning of the statement that "this *yoga* is accomplished."

For the sake of knowledge, the author of the treatise employs the term "perfected" (*siddha*) in the appropriate place. As long as the vessel, the bowl, or the birth [of the substance] remains inscribed with subtle lines, its manifestation does not occur; but when it is extracted and washed, there is liberation. ||100||

Now, regarding the extinguishing of the lamp: "kolaṣkāsa" refers to oil extracted from the *āmra* (mango) fruit and so forth; a lamp made with that [oil] is not disturbed even by a violent wind, but remains perfectly steady. For this very reason, it is like a great jewel-lamp. ||101||
16a) A *mallaka* (bowl) inscribed with *huḍavit* brings about the immobilization of a woman who has recently given birth; it causes her to cry out loudly.
The noble lady Garbhasapadī, through the noble rite of *stambhana* (paralysis), achieved success by means of that name Vidarbhitā. 100.
The lamp of sesame oil, with its wick made of *kokkāsa* fibers, burns brightly even when the wind is fierce.
In the wind, there was a trembling, like a great jewel-lamp flickering. ||101||

The excrement of a sun-cricket (*raviśalabha*) and a lizard (*godhā*), along with realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and yellow myrobalan (*pathyā*), destroy the venom of a scorpion; when applied as an ointment, they cause the sting to burst open. (102)

Now, the removal of scorpion venom: A paste made from the excrement of a sun-insect (*arkakīṭaka*), a house-lizard, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and myrobalan (*harītakī*), ground with water, should be applied to the sting of a scorpion; thus the scorpion venom is destroyed. (102)

It illuminates [the following]: having made a fine powder from the seeds of the *palāśa* tree, one should saturate it twenty-one times with the milk of the *arka* plant; by this, even the poison of a scorpion is destroyed upon being stung.
"Northern" means: one should take the roots of pomegranate trees located in the northern direction and cow-flesh;

having ground these together with water, a pill should be prepared. When a scorpion sting is touched with this pill, the scorpion's venom departs even from the site of the sting; however, when another person is seen, the poison spreads there.
In this very matter, even the gods have praised this pill. || 104 ||
A pill made from mung bean seeds cultivated on a Brahma-tree (brahmataru) that has absorbed the essence of the sun (the sun's rays) quickly destroys the poison of a scorpion when applied. (103)

A pill made from the roots of the northern pomegranate (uttaradāḍima), equal in measure to cow dung and powdered together, is praised even by the gods for use when bitten by the venom of a scorpion. (104)

16b) Regarding *aṅkule*: one should prepare pills from equal parts of *aṅkula* oil, the root of *aṅkula*, the root of pomegranate, pomegranate oil, the root of *jaṃbu*, *jaṃbu* oil, and honey. This is *madhuṣāḍ*. One should make pills with these in equal proportions.
The pill transmits the scorpion venom; that is to say, it causes it to move from one place to another. ||104||
Now, the immobilization of water.

Having smeared the body with the powder of *stabdha* seeds, with the powder of *vothari*, and mixed with the ashes of a forest site, when the cloud rains, the water does not enter his body; by that water he is neither made variegated nor is he soaked—this is the meaning. ||106||
The root of *aṅkola* with oil, and the roots of pomegranate and *jambu* with oil.
A pill made from equal parts of honey and sugar causes the transfer of scorpion venom. ||105||
With the body [anointed] together with ashes and the powder of seeds hardened by jaggery.
By the falling showers of clouds, the wandering [world] is made variegated. ||106||
Regarding the term *sarjarasa*: resin (*sarjarasa*) and the liquid of a metal-smelter (*lohakāra-rasa*) are well known; [and] the sap of the white *arka* flower (*śvetārka-puṣpa-rasa*).
When a cloth has been smeared with these, water is subsequently poured upon that cloth; that water does not adhere to the cloth.
The meaning is that even when being sprinkled with water, it does not become wet. This is manifest to all people. (107)
Thus ends the section on the immobilization of water.
17a) Now,
the method of making oneself invisible.
Harīti says: if there is a breakage in this commentary.
Regarding "puracāṅguli": *pura* is bdellium (*guggulu*), *cāṅgulī* is bamboo manna (*vaṃśalocanā*), *bodhavṛkṣa* is the *śavaṇikā* tree;
its bark, its juice, water, and *airaka*—when these are used to wash and sprinkle a cloth, the practitioner, once that cloth has been treated, cannot be seen even by Daityas, gods, or Gandharvas.
"Moist" is an adjective qualifying the cloth. ||109||
And with the sap smeared from a lacquer tree, iron, and a copper-smelter, as well as with the water from mandāraka flowers.
A manifest cloth, even when being thoroughly sprinkled with water, does not become wet. ||107||
It should be painted on a cloth using pigments mixed with the juice of the roots of the *harītakī* tree.
That which is dry is not seen; that which is visible is moistened by waters.
Having performed the preliminary rites, offered incense, and anointed himself with the juice of the dhatura plant;
Even by asuras, suras, and kinnaras, that cloth, while still wet, cannot be seen once it has been set out. ||109||

Regarding the phrase "dinā" and so forth: the enemy of serpents, the peacock, having fasted for seven days, shall, when the eighth day arrives, eat realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and yellow orpiment (*haritāla*). Then, its excrement should be collected.
When that substance is smeared [on something], even if it has reached the middle of the hand, no one at all will see it.
The meaning is that it becomes unseen. ||110||

"Three days" means: he who has remained without food for three days, having first consumed a mountain-dwelling tortoise or lizard, and subsequently when his excrement has been digested, takes the yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) contained therein and smears it upon the center of his left palm; by means of that smeared hand, he draws out ornaments, such that no one can perceive him as he grasps those ornaments.
It is not seen. ||111||
17b) For seven days he should be maintained [in this state]; he is a bearer of the stone slab, a destroyer of the arms of Māra.
An object smeared with that substance cannot be seen, even when it is held in the palm of one's hand. ||110||
It was practiced for three days by Girikaṣapa and by Tālapāda.
Therefore, having smeared the hollows of his palms with that, he should cast down the ornaments. ||111||
Regarding "the seed": mercury, poison, castor-seed, snake-flesh, and the limb-seed of the *aṅkola* tree are called the "limb-seed.
Having ground these together into one, one should smear the palm of the hand with it; when that [hand] touches the image of a deity or others, the image is then drawn forth. ||112||

"Jīva": by means of these—poison (*viṣa*), *pārijāta* flower, *tālaka*, and the tail of a snake—ground together with *kola* oil and applied to the palm of the hand, the extraction of conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and so forth, occurs. ||113||
The seed [is prepared] with viṣa, āruṣkara, the horn of a goat, and the parts of a lizard, combined with mercury (kūṭa).
By means of these joined with the branch-animals, there occurs the drawing of the image. ||113||
The seed-remover [is countered] by *pārijātaka* and *tāla* [plants], and that of *hālāhala* poison by the tail [of a peacock].
An attraction of conch shells and mother-of-pearl occurs when they are treated with *aṅkola* oil. 113.

"Kacchapa": the head and foot of a *kacchapa* (a specific type of living creature), and *indragopa*—by means of these medicinal substances, oils cooked with them, when applied as an ointment to the breasts of women, effect the removal of the breasts. ||114||
Regarding "girī": *girikarṇikā* is well known. *Indragopa* refers to the centipede (*śatapādika*) and the thousand-legged tree (*sahasracaraṇoka*).

Having combined these together into a powder, it causes the wound of the female organ (*bhaga*) to contract. Other wounds as well heal by means of this powder; therefore, it is called *asaureru*, the king of powders (*cūrṇarāja*). ||115||
A plaster made from tortoise heads, feet, and indragopa insects mixed with cooked oil brings about the disappearance of a woman's breasts when applied. 114.
18a) [The names] Girikarṇika, Indragopaka, Śatāṅghrika, and Hastacaraṇa— thus, from these,
dust and royal filth arise in other excellent limbs as well. (115)

Regarding the term *lalanā*: by the habit of moving and shaking the cow-horn (*gośṛṅga*) which has gone downward, that which is obtained—the dust-powder of that cow-horn—renders the private parts of women and men such that they are no longer accessible for sexual union or service. Likewise, from the application of that same cow-horn which has gone upward to its place, the private parts [of the man] become as before.

The meaning is that *prakṛti* is the one who is to be approached by men. By this, [it is shown that] the woman’s excellent organ possesses contraction and expansion; thus, it is an exceedingly excellent organ. 117.
"Prāmā" means: that ignoble woman who crosses over the thread dyed with the blood of that two-headed serpent; from the opening of her womb, a stream of blood flows forth. ||118||
Lalanā does not become approachable when one wanders through the dust of cow dung due to excessive smearing.
By the application of the powder from the upward-pointing horn, they likewise return to their natural state. ||116||

As he violated the young woman, the white semen, mixed with the blood of his wounds, flowed from his two openings; it was consumed by the hand of her enemy, who had struck him, as it fell into the cavity of her quivering vulva. 117.
Regarding the term "mahiṣī" (buffalo): the root, stem, leaf, flower, and fruit—these are the five parts (*pañcāṅga*) of the thorn-apple (*dhattūra*).

One should take fifteen parts of the powder of these five parts and one sixteenth part of *vatsanāga* poison. Having ground these together into a single powder, it should be smeared with buffalo blood twenty-one times.

Having impregnated it with buffalo blood and dried it in the shade, it is made into incense; by the burning of this incense at night, all activity of a man is destroyed—this is the meaning. Because of the mention of "night," this incense removes [the power] of men only at night, but during the day, nothing [of the sort occurs].
18b) Unclear 19a)

Regarding the phrase "with flowers and barley": having sown various kinds of grain in the skull of a man who has been pierced by a weapon or impaled on a stake under a lunar mansion associated with flowers (*puṣpanakṣatra*), it is irrigated with the milk of a ewe. When fruits of such a nature as those [intended] emerge from those grains thus irrigated, one should take them and give them to a garland-maker.
When the garland is bound upon the head, it "conceals" the practitioner—the man—meaning it renders him invisible.
Regarding the phrase "mṛdvāraṇa" (an elephant made of clay): *mṛt* means clay; that which is produced from it is a clay elephant (*mṛdvāraṇa*).
The hollow or cavity (*randhra*) located in its frontal globe (*kumbhasthala*)—into that, this resinous exudate (*niryāsa*) of the two trees, *picumarda* and *sarja*, has been poured.
The juice of these two trees, through the heat of the sun’s rays, maintains a state of intoxication and playful grace. ||123||

Regarding the phrase "having smeared": having smeared the left foot with the powder of donkey and goat placenta mixed with black pepper, long pepper, and ginger, the tree—being struck—drops all its flowers and fruits;
the meaning is that not even a single flower, fruit, or the like remains on that tree. ||124||
[One should perform the rite] with flowers and barley grains placed in a skull [of a person] pierced by a weapon or a trident.
With the medicinal decoctions of the *āvika* plant, he conceals that fruit within the tethering post. ||122||
Even though its flow issues from the hollows of the frontal globes of a mild-elephant,
this ichor, when touched by the rays of the sun, maintains a playful state of intoxication.
Having cast the left foot [into the fire] with the seed-mantra of the female donkey (rāsabhī) conjoined with the three pungents (trikaṭuka).
Struck by that shower of all kinds of flowers, the tree releases [them]. ||124||

"Spṛṣṭa" means: when a tree is touched by that hand which has been smeared with a powder consisting of the womb of a female dog, along with black pepper (*marīca*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), it releases a multitude of fruits and flowers, like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kāmadruma*) or a *kalpavṛkṣa*. Just as such a tree yields all fruits, flowers, and so forth exactly as requested—
Just as one solicits various tasks, so too does she grant all fruits and flowers at the mere touch of her hand; this is the meaning. ||121||

19b) *Dinā* means: when cow's milk has been poured into a great jar or pot (*ghaṭa*) that has been smeared with the milky sap of the *arka* plant and repeatedly saturated with dried *arka* sap, until it is mixed with one *pala* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). When this excellent [mixture] has been prepared...
That milk does not abandon its state of excellence; thus, all of it appears as similar to cow's ghee once it has been placed—that is, deposited—into that jar. ||126||
Touched by his lotus-hand, which was smeared with the placenta of a female cat and the essence of the three pungent spices.
The tree sheds its mass of fruits and flowers, just like a tree of desire.
In this jar, which has been smeared with the milk of the sun (milk) and combined with one *pala* of clarified butter;
As long as the milk remains excellent, so long is the clarified butter deposited within it.

"Pratyagra" means fresh. That which is the interior—the middle—of such a new jar, having been saturated again with milk and then dried, when water is poured into such a jar, it immediately becomes primarily buttermilk;
the meaning is that the water appears like cow's milk. ||127||

"Repeatedly" (asakṛt) means: in that manner, not indeed in the previously mentioned way; nor [is it] in a jar that has been processed again with the milk of the *arka* plant—this is the meaning. In such a jar, which is joined with the interior of a wood-apple fruit (*kapittha*), that is to say, provided with the dried interior of the wood-apple fruit characterized by its fibrous core—[in such a jar]. ||129||
One should saturate the interior of a fresh jar many times with the milk of the sun.
For as soon as water is poured into it, it indeed becomes buttermilk.
Likewise, when repeatedly smeared with milk and combined with the pulp of dried kapittha fruit, [it becomes soft].
When powdered and applied, it causes buttermilk to turn into the state of curd. ||128||
20a) It approaches. Those [fish] have ceased [to move], they are dead, and they are dried; those are the fish and the sea-monsters.
Of them, there is *āruṣkara*, which is *bhallātaka*; its fruit is smeared with that juice on the flanks of those [beings] who are thus [prepared].

When those [fish] that have been killed are thrown into cool water, they regain life at that very moment; the meaning is that even dead fish, by means of this performed rite, come back to life again. ||129||

Regarding the term "puruṣam" (the man): that stake or peg (*śaṅku-kīlaka*) which comes from the side of a dead man—specifically the bone of a long neck—is cast into the hole or the opening of a camel; it effects the binding of the womb for a man and woman engaged in sexual union. As soon as those two have mounted for the act of love, at that very moment, that peg [enters] there.

If it is inserted into the cavity, then it means that [the seed] emerges from between the penis and the vagina of the man. By drawing [the organ] from the middle of the hole of the unstable stake (śaṅku), the binding of the marks of both man and woman becomes released;
such is the meaning. ||130||
Before long; quickly.
For fish that have been stunned by hooks and dried out, with their sides smeared with the juice of *aruṣkara*, life returns from cold water in the blink of an eye. (129)
The man was soon cast by the two women into the hollow of a long-necked bone.
At the time of sexual union, Mṛtapuruṣayāgośaṅku performs the Varāṅgabandha. 130.
Regarding the term *sarit*: it refers to a river flowing toward the ocean. From its eastern and western banks, one takes earth-clay.

During sexual union, two dogs—*sāramayya-kakkurī*, meaning "essence-filled" or "robust"—become attached and cling to that clay. One takes the hair from those two dogs and, together with the aforementioned clay, forms a pill. This [pill], directed toward whichever man [is the target], is placed in the midst of *aṅkola* oil.
That person is cast down upon whatever seat, stool, bench, elephant, horse, man, chariot, or indeed any other place where he may be standing; right there, he becomes a stake.
The meaning is that his seat and other such items rise up together with the one who is joined [to him].
When the pill is drawn out from the oil, the seat and so forth become released. ||131||
The hairs on the bodies of the dogs, who were emaciated from eating the mud on both banks of the river.
This pill, which causes all postures and bonds to adhere when licked, is prepared with Kaula oil. 131. Śrī. Śrī.
Śrī.

Regarding the phrase "by the eyes": the pair of eyes (nayana-yuga) [is the means]; through them, for practitioners who have practiced the lunar orb (*caṇḍramaṇḍala*) upon the letter *bha* situated in the center of the rays, the light situated within—that is, inside—the body becomes manifest as a dense darkness. Through meditation on such a syllable, [this occurs] for the practitioner.
The meaning is that the light which illuminates the entire mass of objects of knowledge is now fully unfolding. ||132||
The rays of the pair of eyes [become] the light in the center through the practice of the moon-maṇḍala.
Likewise, the inner light named Nārāyaṇa manifests even in the midst of darkness.

Concluding the treatise, he says: "From the mouth of the guru. That which is the desired thorough knowledge from the mouth—the lotus face—of the gurus, which was taught by the well-pleased gurus to me in private; that I have known, having attained within it the verse of direct experience.
The meaning is "having experienced. From among those [teachings] that have come down through the path of authentic experience,
this *Āścaryayogaratnāvalī* treatise— which is slightly inferior, being only a small portion—
has been seen and made public here in this *Mukhāvabodha-bandha*.
Thus, by this [work], the venerable teacher Nāgārjuna reveals himself. ||133||
21a) And whatever other treatises have been learned by me from the mouth of the guru and elsewhere;
Having brought my experience before me, I have seen something here from within that [experience].

"Āścarya" (Marvel): Marvels themselves are the jewels; their garland is the sequence composed and strung together by the master Nāgārjuna. Of what nature is it? It is established through experience (*anubhava-prasiddhā*). Furthermore, for those people who possess the sixty-four arts (*kalās*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*), [this is the case].
The heart is the internal organ; its beloved is the *Āścaryayogamālā*. O Suvrata, it has been completed through the medium of one hundred and forty sūtras.
With the words "It triumphs," the Teacher offers a benediction for the treatise, signifying that it shines forth with supreme excellence. (134)
The *Āścaryayogamālā*, composed by Nāgārjuna and renowned through personal experience, which is dear to the hearts of all people, triumphs as it is established by means of its essential verses. 134.

"For the sake of self-remembrance": whatever has been described by the Teacher here that is impure, let that be forgiven; having bestowed grace upon me, let it be purified—for who does not stumble through the force of negligence?
In the year twelve hundred and six of the illustrious King Vikrama’s era, this was composed by Guṇākara, a mendicant from Śvetāmbara; may it be victorious! ||135||
Thus ends the *Āścaryayogamālā-laghuvṛtti* composed by the venerable Śvetāmbara scholar Guṇākara.
This *Āścaryayogamālā* composed by Nāgārjuna has been sold by me for my own remembrance; it stands before you, O Elder, as a commentary. (135)
May Śrī Kumbheśvara be ever victorious! Śrī!
Thus ends the *Āścaryayogamālā*. May there be well-being.
The *Adbhutayogamālā* was indeed written at the place of Kumbheśvara.
And by Bhavānīśaṅkara, the son of Gaṇeśabhaṭṭa. || 1 ||
That which has indeed been taken by fraud must not be given to anyone at all.
The earth is difficult to find; let it not fall into the hands of the wicked—will I not take it away? ||1||
Beholding all those people qualified in the science of grammar, he, possessing a nature of compassion, drank [the nectar] that was beyond the reach of enemies.
One who is devoid of all auspiciousness,
who speaks ill of others,
who is envious during the performance of the Upākarma rite, and likewise at a Śrāddha for the deceased;
And during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, no fault from dust exists. ||1||
The Kauśikī, Vāgmatī, Gaṅgā, and Gaṇḍakī rivers, which arise from Dharma, are not defiled by the impurities of menstrual blood. ||2||
That river, [emerging] from the mouth of Rudra, is not defiled by the impurities of dust.
The Vāgmatī, who is venerable as Sarasvatī, [flows] for three days after the month of Karkaṭaka.
Between the signs of Leo and Cancer, all rivers are subject to their menstrual flow.
One should not bathe in them, except for those rivers that flow to the ocean. ||1||
If pure sesame oil is added to rice gruel and drunk, there will be an arrest of semen.
